## 1. Overview {#sec-overview}

Peritoneal dialysis (PD) is associated with improved patient autonomy, quality of life, and lower healthcare utilization in selected populations. Despite these advantages, only a minority of U.S. patients with end-stage kidney disease initiate PD  (\~ 12%). Patients who start on hemodialysis and subsequently transition to PD ("PD-switch") represent a particularly important subgroup, as prior studies suggest they may experience higher risks of technique failure and mortality compared with patients who initiate dialysis directly with PD. Understanding sociodemographic factors associated with initial dialysis modality pathway may identify potentially modifiable barriers to PD uptake and inform future quality improvement interventions.

Repo Link: <https://github.com/betancojmd/BMIN5030_Final_Project/tree/juan_project>

## 2. Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Few studies have examined sociodemographic factors associated with the pathway by which patients ultimately receive peritoneal dialysis. Most prior research has focused on clinical outcomes after PD initiation rather than factors influencing whether patients begin dialysis with PD or transition from hemodialysis later.

This project leverages a contemporary institutional PD registry to identify potentially modifiable disparities in access to PD. Findings may inform practical and scalable interventions, such as enhanced predialysis education, earlier nephrology referral, and targeted outreach to underserved populations.

My hypothesis is that patients initiating dialysis directly with PD differ from patients who transition from hemodialysis to PD with respect to sociodemographic characteristics, including age, race, ethnicity, employment status, mobility, and prior nephrology care.

## 3. Methods {#sec-methods}

## 3.1 Data (Information Retrieval) {#sec-data}

**Data source:** Electronic Health Records (EPIC) and [CMS-2728 Form](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/cms-forms/cms-forms/cms-forms-items/cms008867) (End Stage Renal Disease Medical Evidence Report) which provides a snapshot of individuals with ESRD AT THE TIME OF DIALYSIS INITIATION. Data were obtained from a de-identified registry developed for a quality improvement initiative approved by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Review Board on March 11, 2025.

**Subjects/Cohort:** All adult patients receiving peritoneal dialysis within the University of Pennsylvania renal practice between January 1, 2025 and December 31, 2025 (N = 91).

**Study design:** Retrospective observational cohort study and quality improvement project based on electronic health record review.

**Primary Outcome:** Dialysis initiation pathway: PD-first (direct initiation with peritoneal dialysis) vs PD-switch (transition from in-center hemodialysis to peritoneal dialysis).

## 3.2 Variables and Data Dictionary {#sec-variables}

**Quantitative Continuous**

-Total Dialysis Vintage and PD Vintage (exact years)

**Quantitative** **Discrete**

-Age (whole years)

**Categorical** **Nominal**

-First Dialysis Modality: PD first (CAPD or CCPD) vs PD switch (ICHD) (0. Hemodialysis 1.CAPD 2. CCPD 3.Other)

-ZIP code

-Dialysis Unit (n=3)

-Race (0:American Indian or Alaska Native, 1: Asian, 2:Black or African American, 3:Middle Eastern or North African, 4:Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, 5: White, 6:Multiracial, 7:Other/unknown)

-Prior or Current employment at dialysis initiation (0.unemployed 1.Full Time 2.Part Time 3.Homemaker 4.Retired due to age/preference 5.Retired (Disability) 6.Medical Leave 7.Student)

-Dialysis access (0.AVF 1.AVG 2.Catheter 3.Other 4. PDC) -Dialysis setting (0. Home 1.Dialysis facility 3.SNF/LTAC)

-Type of home dialysis training (0. HHD 1. ICHD 2. CAPD 3. CCPD 4. Other 5.PD (not specified if CAPD or CCPD)

-Nephrologist (n=17)

**Ordinal**

-Established nephrologist (0.No 1.Yes 2.Unknown)

-Time with Nephrologist (0. \<6mo 1.6-12 mo 2.\>12mo 3.not applicable)

-Co-morbid conditions (0.inability to ambulate 1. inability to transfer 2.needs assistance with daily activities 3. institutionalized 4.vision impairment 5. drug dependence 6.none of the above)

**Binary**

-Sex assigned at birth (0.Male, 1.Female)

-Ethnicity (0:Non-Hispanic, 1:Hispanic)

-Medicare application? (0.No 1.Yes)

-Transplant information provided? (0.No 1.Yes)

## 3.3 Data cleaning

```{r}
#Will first summarize variable names, types and first few values
#str(pd_data)

#Had to recode dialysis_type variable into PD first vs PD switch 

pd <- pd_data %>%
  mutate(
    dialysis_type = case_when(
      dialysis_type == 0 ~ "PD switch",
      dialysis_type %in% c(1, 2) ~ "PD first",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    dialysis_type = factor(dialysis_type, levels = c("PD first", "PD switch"))
  )


#In order to calculate total dialysis vintage and peritoneal dialysis vintage in years will use dplyr and lubridate packages 

#First will confirm that the dialysis initiation dates were not date objects but  POSIXct 

class(pd$date_chronic_dialysis_initiated)
head(pd$date_chronic_dialysis_initiated)

#Then had to  strip the time component and convert them cleanly into standard Date objects.

pd <- pd %>%
  mutate(
    date_chronic_dialysis_initiated = as.Date(date_chronic_dialysis_initiated),
    home_dialysis_date_training_pdc_placement = as.Date(home_dialysis_date_training_pdc_placement))
    
#Then will Calculate vintage in years  by taking the time interval between each start date and December 31, 2025.
pd <- pd %>%
    mutate(
    total_dialysis_vintage = time_length(
      interval(date_chronic_dialysis_initiated, as.Date("2025-12-31")), 
      unit = "years"
    ),
    pd_vintage = time_length(
      interval(home_dialysis_date_training_pdc_placement, as.Date("2025-12-31")), 
      unit = "years"
    )
  )

#Then will use summary function to visualize snapshot of these new variables
head(tibble(pd$total_dialysis_vintage))
head(tibble(pd$pd_vintage))

```

```{r}

#Given that many categorical variables showed as numeric and viceversa, had to transform them appropriately

pd_clean <- pd %>% mutate(across(c(dialysis_unit,sex,race,ethnicity,medicare_application,prior_employement,current_employement,co_morbid_conditions,nephrologist,time_nephrologist,access,dialysis_setting,dialysis_type,kidney_txp_information,name_nephrologist,type_of_training), as.factor))


```

```{r}
#initially I attempted using the tidyr::drop_na() command to get a set of complete cases for a dataset (dropping all samples with missing data), however this dropped sample population in half (n=91) down to (n=46) so decided to keep original data frame with missing values for the analysis
```

**Univariate Analysis:** a) Continuous variables: Mean ± standard deviation or median (IQR), Student's t-test, b) Categorical variables: Frequencies and percentages, Chi-square test or Fisher's exact test
